To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

capsaicinoinduced currents and two types of pH‐sensitive currents are accompanied by a change of the fura‐2 fluorescence signal that depends on extracellular Ca2+, and that the fractional contribution of the Ca2+-current to the total current is significantly different for capasaicin- and proton‐induced current types.
the fraction of Ca2+ current through capsaicin- and proton-gated ion channels is different and that the fraction of current through proton-gated ion channel increases with increasing pH.
Capsaicin and proton‐induced membrane currents in DRG neurons are accompanied by a Ca2+ influx.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Ca2+ in capsaicin- and proton-activated ion channels and the functional consequences of Ca2+ influx for primary nociceptive neurons.
the role of Ca2+ in the activation and sensitization of nociceptive aural neurones.
the role of the Ca2+-activated potassium channel in regulating the excitability of nociceptive neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
capsaicins and proton‐activated currents are different, but both are non‐selective and both can be Ca2+ selective.
capsaicinoinduced and slowly inactivatin proton-induced current are different.
capsaicine and protons activate the same channels but that the fraction of Ca2+ is different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the capsaicin receptor (VR1) and the proton receptor are different proteins.
the two stimuli capsaicin (a vanilloid) and protons (H+) activate ion channels which may be important for the sensitization of primary afferents.
capsaicino‐ and slowly inactiving proton‐induced current are carried by different channels and that the Ca2+ influx via these channels is important for the sensitization of nociceptive aferents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we were able to measure the fraction of the whole‐ cell current that was carried by calcium.
capsaicinoinduced currents are significantly more permeable to calcium ions than are proton‐induced current.
the two stimuli (protons and capsaicsin) activate different populations of channels.
